items.title: Germany's Isar Aerospace launches rocket into orbit from Norway
items.summary: Germany's Isar Aerospace launched a rocket into orbit from Norway on Saturday as Europe races to boost its ability to economically send satellites into space independently of the United States.

items.title: Indonesia’s most dangerous fires are burning underground
items.summary: Indonesia’s dangerous peat fires are surging early in the 2026 fire season as a strengthening El Niño and severe drought dry out wetlands that can burn underground for months. items.title: Haze emergency grips Malaysian Borneo town
items.summary: Acrid smoke hung heavily over the Malaysian town of Serian, seeping into homes and cloaking roadside stalls, as residents navigated an air-quality emergency fueled by transboundary haze from Indonesia's raging fires.

items.title: AI can now control fusion plasma faster than humans can react
items.summary: Princeton researchers have tested an AI system that can monitor and control fusion plasma in milliseconds, reacting far faster than a human operator. In one experiment, it predicted a damaging instability about 200 milliseconds before it appeared and adjusted the plasma to stop it from forming.

items.title: Scientists find a weak spot in one of the deadliest brain cancers
items.summary: Researchers may have found a new way to weaken glioblastoma’s defenses against treatment. Blocking a protein called SET prevented tumors from forming in preclinical models, while targeting related proteins made cancer cells more vulnerable to radiation. items.title: A mysterious signal around Earth could be dark matter
items.summary: Scientists used Earth’s magnetic field and atmosphere as a planet-sized detector to search for some of the lightest proposed forms of dark matter. The approach dramatically improved limits on ultralight axions and uncovered several intriguing dark photon signals that still need to be explained.

items.title: 80,000-year-old “arrowheads” rewrite human history
items.summary: Archaeologists have identified tiny 80,000-year-old projectile points in Uzbekistan that may have been used like arrowheads. items.title: Heart disease and kidney disease can fuel each other. New guidelines aim to break the cycle
items.summary: Heart disease and chronic kidney disease can accelerate one another, but new guidelines say simple screening and early treatment could substantially reduce the risks. items.title: This “new” frog was hiding in plain sight for 100 years
items.summary: A common frog found across Ecuador and Colombia has finally been recognized as its own species after more than a century of mistaken identity. Museum specimens from the 1800s helped scientists reveal that Pristimantis milpe had been hiding in plain sight all along.

items.summary: Conformational changes in proteins are vital to their function yet remain challenging for state-of-the-art artificial intelligence, such as AlphaFold3, to predict. items.title: How much clearcutting can nature sustain? A study determines the ecological limit for boreal forest birds
items.summary: A study led by the University of Jyväskylä in Finland evaluated, for the first time, an ecological threshold for the amount of clearcutting in boreal forests. items.title: Compound in blueberries may help muscle cells burn excess fat
items.summary: Scientists in Japan have identified a natural compound found in blueberries, grapes, and other berries that may help muscle cells burn excess fat instead of storing it. items.title: FAST finds two mysterious hydrogen clouds with no visible stars
items.summary: Astronomers have found two clouds of hydrogen near the Whirlpool galaxy that appear to contain almost no stars. items.summary: The human-animal bond is often so strong that pet owners may delay or forgo medical treatment or leave a health care facility against medical advice if they have no one to care for their pet at home. items.title: US study tests psilocybin to fight cancer side effects
items.summary: Here's a novel idea for countering the painful side effects of chemotherapy: Beforehand, take the hallucinogenic drug found in magic mushrooms.

items.title: A black hole as light as 40 tons can exist inside a star if dark matter helps
items.summary: In 1974, Stephen Hawking made a prediction that transformed our understanding of black holes. Black holes, he showed, are not truly black: They slowly lose energy through a quantum process now known as Hawking radiation. The lighter the black hole, the faster it evaporates.

items.title: Tree species diversity protects forests from climate extremes, study finds
items.summary: New research has found that tree species diversity can play a crucial role in protecting forests from the growing threat of extreme climate events. items.title: Scientists discover how narwhals grow nature's only straight tusk
items.summary: Narwhals have nature's only straight tusk, a single tooth up to three meters (10 feet) long, so strange they were sold as magical unicorn horns during the Middle Ages.

items.title: Some disagreement makes groups more trustworthy, mathematical framework finds
items.summary: When humans are making decisions, they are known not to rely solely on their own considerations and the evidence available to them. Past behavioral science and psychology studies have shown that people are often also influenced by the choices and opinions of others.

items.title: Lakes aren't just storing water—they're changing the carbon cycle
items.summary: Lakes may look like picturesque stopping points along a river or stream, but they can have a big influence on what happens to carbon as it moves through a landscape. items.summary: Has El Niño reached the West Coast? You might think it has. After all, the ocean off Southern and Central California is unusually warm. items.title: Late Roman decrees uncover military system behind amphitheater animal spectacles
items.summary: A study on Roman law by the Carlos III University of Madrid analyzes the regulations and complex imperial logistics governing the capture, transport and safety of animals used in spectacles in the Roman Empire—which were far more popular than gladiatorial combat.

items.title: New method predicts where massive earthquakes will strike
items.summary: UC Riverside scientists have developed a way to identify where Earth's biggest earthquakes are most likely to occur, offering a powerful new tool for improving disaster preparation in some of the most dangerous seismic regions.

items.title: How haze from Indonesian fires impacts Southeast Asia
items.summary: Thick smog has blanketed parts of Indonesia as the vast archipelago battles fires that have burned large swaths of Borneo and Sumatra for weeks.

items.title: Indonesia rescues second orangutan mother and baby from wildfire
items.summary: An orangutan mother and her baby, threatened by wildfires encroaching on their habitat in Indonesia, were rescued earlier this week, authorities said in a statement Saturday.

items.title: Spacecraft bound for Mercury begins 'tricky' arrival
items.summary: After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the monthslong, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the sun-scorched planet.

items.title: Levitated magnet opens new frontier in search for ultraheavy dark matter
